Review 7 (rated 2/5): "Having found myself rather disappointed by my brief forays into the Young Adult genre, I decided to find the people who had read the most teen books and discover what they viewed as the best of the best. The name Laini Taylor kept popping up, and this book was pointed to as "gorgeous", with flowery language and beautiful characters. 
 If this is what qualifies as flowery writing, I sure don't want to see dull writing. 
 For the first 100 pages, this novel hits the right rhythm; we feel that the story is progressing while Taylor still maintains the everyday rhythm of life. Try "The Westing Game" or "Watership Down" for a mastery of this style. Lazlo as a character is perfectly likeable, but suffers from Protagonist-itis; i.e. "The Luke Skywalker Syndrome". He's boring. He does all the necessary heroic things, but there's no edge to this character, there's no subtleties. He's just a good person, with no immediate flaws, and nothing much to learn. 
 We get an intriguing blend of mystery and story, but the cracks soon appear. We're introduced to a set of half-human children who act like regular 14-year-old modern teenagers. We're thrown lots of unnecessary detail about the creatures of this world. We're given dozens of made-up names. We're given dull, dull, dull prose. 
 I mean, some of the writing is just ugly . She'll introduce some interesting concept, then immediately ruin it. 
 And so the dreamer and the goddess went shopping for a moon. 
 Okay, fine so far. 
 It was like something out of a story. Well, it was like something out of a dream. 
 There, she's just ruined the atmosphere. This is basic show-don't-tell stuff. If you're going to try to create an otherworldly atmosphere, don't break the moon-shopping excursion with, "Well, it was like something out of a dream." 
 Some of the book sounds like a teenage girl's diary. 
 He really, really, really wanted to kiss her 
 Are you kidding me? 
 Taylor soon does what I was fearing. She drops one-hundred pages of soppy romance straight onto her promising plot and drowns the (quite interesting!) ethical dillema in a thick soup of sentimentality. I have no problem with romance, as long as it isn't presented as rainbows and butterflies and kisses, "EVERYTHING IS PERFECT" romance, and this is exactly what I feared. These characters have no problems together, they just fall in love on first sight. It's an unrealistic romance that once again sends the message to readers that 'true love' is all about bliss and has no work or sacrifice involved. Ultimately, it's just cheap. 
 At about page 460, she realizes all of a sudden that she needs a climax. There are many explosions. 
 So the writing. Everyone talked about how beautiful it was, saying it was too metaphorical for some readers! I just didn't see it. Mostly it was just plain old, "He did, she said, there was..." stuff. Occasionally she'd try out a simile or metaphor, but there was nothing to stir the imagination, nothing to provoke wonder. 
 Beautiful writing is not sappy writing. This, "I think you're a fairy tale. I think you're magical, and brave, and exquisite. And I hope you'll let me be in your story." isn't beautiful writing. Throwing abstract similes like, blue as five murders waiting to happen is just incoherent. When I hear about beautiful metaphorical writing, I'm thinking about maybe something out of Peake. 
 The crumbling castle, looming among the mists, exhaled the season, and every cold stone breathed it out. The tortured trees by the dark lake burned and dripped, their leaves snatched by the wind were whirled in wild circles through the towers. The clouds mouldered as they lay coiled, or shifted themselves uneasily upon the stone skyfield, sending up wreathes that drifted through the turrets and swarmed up hidden walls. 
 or maybe Proust! 
 But sometimes illumination comes to our rescue at the very moment when all seems lost; we have knocked at every door and they open on nothing until, at last, we stumble unconsciously against the only one through which we can enter the kingdom we have sought in vain a hundred years - and it opens. 
 Is it unfair to compare Laini Taylor to Proust or Peake? Sure, of course it is. But this book obviously tried at times to reach some level of metaphorical resonance and descriptive ecstasy. Why water it down? Why not go full out? Why not reach for the skies? 
 And here's the main reason I disliked the book; it was drowning in potential. The characters were there, the plot was there, the setting was there...but the execution fell short. Still, it covered the bases, and it wasn't boring, so I'll give her that. I'll read the sequel when it comes out, and hope that it does a better job exploring the places this story could go."

Laini Taylor is an amazing story teller. I love her vivid descriptions. I loved it in her Daughter of Smoke and Bone series and I loved it equally as well here. There were definitely some parts to the book that didn't sit well with me, but I don't think I was as disappointed by others. 
 What didn't sit well with me at all was how babies were basically seen as property. Maybe it's because I have an almost 4 months old daughter, and the experience of pregnancy is fresh in my mind. When I would read about how the girls were given drugs to prevent the mother/baby bond during pregnancy and they referred to babies as "deliveries" or "preggs," I found myself feeling upset.  Another part of the story that bothered me was how the teens were encouraged and paid to have sex and get pregnant. I can't imagine a time when it would be okay for teens to have these masSEX parties trying to get pregnant. Or when it would be acceptable to use Tocin to facilitate sex when one of the partners wasn't quite ready. 
 Even though these parts of the story bothered me, they still made me think. That's the only reason I liked this book. The whole concept of teens being the only fertile part of the population really got me thinking. Could society really end up like that someday? The virus that led to the infertility, could it be caused by something we do now? Is there much difference between surrogates of present day and the surrogates in the book other than age?

 In a world where adults lose fertility around the age of 20 due to a virus, Melody is one of the first girls in her class to go pro, as in professional surrogate. Offered a highly lucrative contact to preg for a well-to-do couple, all she has to do is wait for them to find the perfect match for her. Then her long-lost, "Godfreaky" twin sister, Harmony, shows up wanting her to give up pregging for money and move to Goodside, the religious compound, with her. However, when the surrogate parents finally find the perfect donor, things begin to change for the twins in an unexpected way. 
 I feel like this book was saying a whole lot of things. I also feel like most of things went over my head as I was distracted by the onslaught of pregnancy related slang. The sheer amount of it almost overwhelmed me. Since society has now become focused on encouraging teenage girls to become pregnant, of course the slang would move along with it. It made me laugh but it also made me scratch my head occasionally. And if I had a nickel for every time the word "bump" was used, well, then I'd have a lot of nickels. 
 Still this is a very clever book. In fact, everything about this book screamed clever. It is a biting look at society's tendencies to go overboard with an idea and also to commercialize it. From the FunBump available for the "pre-bumped" to the use of "man brands" (sperm donors), everything about this society is focused on surrogates and child birthing. And I mean everything. I had a hard time grasping the timeline of when all the adults went sterile but everything in the books seemed a bit frantic like babies had to be had now or the world would end. And, by making teenage pregnancy not only palatable but extremely desirable, the message of why they were doing it becomes lost in the marketing. 
 As for the characters, I can't say I liked either one of the twins that much. They represent two extremes and it's hard to relate to an extreme. In fact, the only likable character is Zen, the friend of Melody, who acts like the only voice of reason in the whole book. Everyone is a caricature from both Melody and Harmony down to every adult and teenager in the book with the exception of Zen. Nothing in the whole book felt real and I was emotionally separated from the characters' plights, much like the pregnant teenagers from their bumps. 
 It is a quirky and interesting book though. I found myself racing through it, curious to see what happens next. Was I surprised by the turn of events near the end of the book? No, not really. Am I curious to see what happens next? Yes, actually I am. There were things that could possibly develop into something interesting for the characters and I'd like to see if they are addressed and how so. A lot of people really like this book and I'm still trying to decide how I feel about it. It was worth reading and I guess that's the best thing I can say."

--- COMMUNITY REVIEWS FOR BOOK B: "Rook" ---
Community Average Rating: 3.77/5

Review 1 (rated 4/5): "A fun retelling of The Scarlet Pimpernel. If you liked that story, you'll enjoy this one."

Review 2 (rated 4/5): "In this YA novel, the ghost of the Scarlet Pimpernel rises in the form of the Red Rook. The Scarlet Pimpernel by Baroness Orczy is a classic and one of my all-time favorites, full of romance and espionage in the midst of the French Revolution. Sharon Cameron has cleverly taken the same basic premise and written Rook with a creative dystopian flavor. 
 Set in the far distant future in what remains of England and France, a teenage girl must marry for money to save her family home. The chosen groom is a wealthy, vain, and shallow cousin of one of the most powerful men in Paris. Or is he? And is she just a pretty and impoverished girl being sacrificed for the family heritage? 
 Humorous dialogue and vivid imagery boost this book above normal YA offerings. It takes a lot for a YA novel to impress this old lady, and although it was a slow build, the last half of the book had me hooked and chained!"

Review 3 (rated 5/5): "Rook is a swashbuckling adventure story set in a distant future UK and Paris where all technology is considered "mythical" and the terror of guillotine (now called a razor) is back in full force. 
 A young girl named Sophia, supported by her family and friends, secretes out prisoners of the repressive Parisian regime under the guise of a man called "The Rook." When she isn't masquerading as the Rook, she is hoping that her arranged marriage to a wealthy Parisian named Rene Hasard will help rescue her family's estate (and continue her secret work). 
 When Sophia and Rene finally meet, they find themselves both helplessly attracted to one another, yet not able to trust their feelings or each others motives. Neither Sophie or Renee are what they seem, and as they begin a dangerous and exciting dance towards each other this may mean certain death under the Razor's blade, especially when Sophia's brother is arrested as the Rook and they plan to rescue him. 
 Sort of a blend between The Scarlet Pimpernel, The Tale of Two Cities, and classic YA Dystopia, Rook impressed the hell out of me. Sophia is an excellent female character. She is strong, resourceful, witty, and able to take care of business. Rene is her foil - charming, suave, yet with his own secrets. Their banter and sexual tension is A-MAZ-ING, and I love how the ending played out (no typical YA fare there). 
 Rook is completely self contained in this one novel, bravo to Cameron who could easily have turned this into a trilogy. Since it is one book, I did find the world building a bit on the light side (I was a little confused about the pseudo religion that came a bit out of nowhere for me), but with everything else being so excellent, I didn't even care while reading. There is a nice author note at the end explaining Cameron's thought and logic on this world and was really appreciated. 
 Also, this is who I kept picturing as Rene (although a bit less refined): 
 Highly recommend."

Review 4 (rated 2/5): "Look at the pretty book cover. I am kind of in love with it, not gonna lie. 
 That being said, that's about all I was in love with. 
 Which is a shame, because this book is somewhat unique. It's set in an unspecified, far-off future, but because at some point technology started failing on a global level, mankind has turned back to the days before any kind of technology. They now refer to our present as the Time Before. Plus, the French Revolution part II seems to be in full swing, there are spies and beheadings galore, and in Great Britain (or the Commonwealth, as it's referred to) they have sought solace in celebrating everything Regency. It reads like a historical novel, but it's actually a futuristic/dystopian kind of thing. I don't even know how to shelve this. 
 Which really intigued me, to be honest. I thought this book sounded amazing. And I still think that. I still think that the idea at the basis of all of this was actually a pretty good one. What just didn't work for me was the pacing of the storytelling. The writing style is hard to describe, because it isn't exactly bad, it's just...boring. Even the action sequences are told in a way that isn't gripping at all, there is too much description and when I started this I kept losing focus. I actually fell asleep a few times at the beginning stage, even though I wasn't reading late at night. And I'm not particularly exhausted because I've just had what is essentially a month-long vacation, so this book quite literally put me to sleep. 
 It did pick up a little at some point, and I admit to really enjoying the relationship between Rene and Sophia. I was drawn to that, but it wasn't enough to overcome the flow and density of the writing, which just didn't work for me. 
 I started skimming very large sections around the 40% mark because this book is just far too long. The idea of history repeating itself and everything coming full circle at some point was intriguing, but homage to The Scarlet Pimpernel or not, the book still remains a bit of a hot mess that could've been great but isn't. 
 The cover, though! So pretty."

Review 8 (rated 4/5): "I received a free copy of this book from the publisher in exchange for an honest review. 
 Everything I loved about "The Scarlet Pimpernel" and more! 
 I am huge fan of "The Scarlet Pimpernel." I enjoy it so much that I wrote a 4000-word paper about it and didn't complain once. Okay... I complained, but can you blame me? 4000 words! In order to write the paper, I read the book three times, took detailed notes (on flashcards) and outlined four possible essay topics. It's safe to say that I know "The Scarlet Pimpernel" pretty damn well.Admittedly, when I added "Rook" to my TBR because it had a pretty cover with the Eiffel Tower on it, and at the time I didn't know it was a retelling of "The Scarlet Pimpernel." But can you imagine my joy when I found out? 
 "Rook" exceeded my expectations of a retelling of the classic tale. Sharon Cameron clearly loves "The Scarlet Pimpernel" as much as I do, because her characters, plot, everything stays so true to the spirit of the original story.Reading "Rook" was like taking a photo with a fish-eye lens. Every element of the original moment is there, rendered in sharp details and vibrant color, but the edges are warped into something new and creative. I got caught up in the story of Sophia, but at the same time I couldn't stop experiencing these moments when I noticed a particular element of the story and thought, "I see what you did there." 
 Cameron cleverly incorporated elements from "The Scarlet Pimpernel," such as the distinctive rescue in the opening chapter, the "foppish" facade of the secretly genius hero and the manipulative ways of the antagonist, in a way that is just similar enough to be recognizable but not so much that she stifles her own creativity. 
 Writing style and narration 
 There seems to be a unanimous complaint of varying degrees on Goodreads about the writing in "Rook." Some say it is too wordy. Others say it makes the story drag.While I can understand where those thoughts are coming from -- the writing style did slow me down a bit, especially during the first few chapters -- I think it was a wonderful and daring decision to make. The writing gives the story a distinctively classic and historic feel.I also have to disagree with comments on the multiple POVs -- "too many!" "so confusing!" -- because Orczy wrote multiple POVs in "The Scarlet Pimpernel," and an homage to the classic wouldn't quite be the same without the internal cliffhangers and dramatic irony. 
 The Scarlet Pimpernel Red Rook and his her league 
 One of the changes I love the most in "Rook" is that, this time, the masked rescuer is female. Sophia Bellamy is clever and brave just like The Scarlet Pimpernel, but she has some of Marguerite's qualities as well. Sophia has the same dedication to saving the innocent that made people love Percy Blakeney. And while Sophia is certainly less conforming of her ladylike roles than Marguerite, the two woman share the same spirit and willingness to risk their lives for their loved ones, especially their brothers, Armand (Marguerite's) and Tom (Sophia's).The Red Rook's league is just as spectacular as The Scarlet Pimpernel's. Or rather, more so. Sophia's rag-tag group of teens is heroic, talented and crazy awesome. I absolutely adored Cartier and the twins!AND THE FOX! THE FOX IS NAMED ST. JUST, AFTER MARGUERITE AND ARMAND! 
 ROMANCE! 
 I'd be totally lying if I said that the romance between Percy and Marguerite were not a big reason for my love of "The Scarlet Pimpernel." But the romance between Sophia and Rene blows theirs away!As it turns out, Sophia isn't the only one hiding something from her fiance. Rene acts like a complete and utter fool. Sound familiar? *pointed look at Percy Blakeney* And while he manages to fool Sophia for a little while, it's not long before she stops buying his foppish act. Too bad she can'f figure him out.Sophia and Rene remind me a lot of Kestrel and Arin in "The Winner's Curse" in that they are both extremely clever and full of secrets. Every interaction between them is a challenge, a game of wits. I love all of the scenes they have together because the tension is so palpable and their feelings for each other, whether it's love, lust or wonder, are so strong. They are absolutely perfect for each other.There was a love triangle *sigh*. Spear Hammond is certainly a complex character. And, while I was certain that he would do anything for Sophia, I constantly wondered, "Can I trust him?" I think he's a great, perplexing character and a valuable addition to the story, but I didn't love him as a love interest. 
 The world they live in 
 This story takes the phrase, "history repeats itself," very literally. In fact, that was the idea that inspired the plot in the first place. The setting, post-apocalyptic Europe, was an interesting change from the setting of "The Scarlet Pimpernel." I'm not completely sold on the fact that the people in "Rook" have reverted their lifestyles to match that of the "ancients," but the revolution is worryingly plausible. After all, France is in its fifth republic.The world of "Rook" was caused by the shift of the earth's poles, and the magnetic disruption basically caused an apocalypse. There are no electronics, no twenty-four hour days and plastic is a rare and ancient treasure. 
 While I think the setting is creative and well-suited for the story, I wish I were provided a little more background. 
 Bottom line 
 "Rook" is a true and brilliant homage to "The Scarlet Pimpernel." It captures the heroic spirit of the classic tale perfectly, borrowing elements both big and little and using them in a whole new way. This story sounds like a historical fiction, looks like a sci-fi and feels like an adventure.The protagonist, Sophia, is daring and dedicated. She's definitely make Percy proud. The romance is full of tension and friendly (or not?) challenges of wit. I absolutely adore Rene Hasard!Whether or not you've read "The Scarlet Pimpernel" -- but especially if you have -- you need to give this book a shot.

Review 1 (rated 3/5): "This is a charming little tea cake of a book - sweet, delicious and ultimately a treat, not a meal. The character of the queen is delightful; a sensible no-nonsense woman who becomes familiar with the ways of the world only when she begins reading books (I found myself hoping that the real Queen has exactly this temperament), and the details about the oddness of her world are lovely, and of course, any reader would be delighted by how much reverence is given to reading itself. I found myself starting to wish there was more given of the world outside of the queens books, but that being said this is a lovely little book."

Review 2 (rated 1/5): "Meh! :/"

Review 6 (rated 3/5): "A book about the pleasure of reading, so it's why I was attracted to it at first, and as it is the Queen of England who is the protagonist, I thought is could be really funny.

Review 7 (rated 2/5): "1.5 stars. 
 I feel oddly guilty writing this review as a book lover. However, I found this book about loving books unbearably pretentious and wholly tedious to read. The constant name dropping of authors and the (blatant) implication that readers see the world not only differently, but also exponentially more accurately than nonreaders, was akin to reading self affirmation phrases over and over again. The entire book suggests that the reader, as a reader, is making himself or herself better than everyone else by engaging in the activity of reading. It felt to me like being constantly and heavy handedly bludgeoned by "intellectual" propaganda. And while I may agree with some of the ideas behind this propaganda, I find a book, not literary or enlightening in the least, about those ideas to be almost offensive.

Review 8 (rated 4/5): "Several people had recommended The Uncommon Reader to me over the last year, but somehow I only got around to it this morning. Don't be as slow as I was! The idea is very simple - the Queen gets hooked on reading - but Bennett handles it perfectly. It's a delight, and takes about an hour to read. 
 Maybe a short extract will do the job:'Exploded?' said the Queen. 'But it was Anita Brookner.' 
 The young man, who seemed remarkably undeferential, said security may have thought it was a device. 
 The Queen said: 'Yes. That is exactly what it is. A book is a device to ignite the imagination.' 
 The footman said: 'Yes, ma'am.' 
 It was as if he was talking to his grandmother, and not for the first time the Queen was made unpleasantly aware of the hostility her reading seemed to arouse. 
 'Very well,' she said. 'Then you should inform security that I shall expect to find another copy of the same book, vetted and explosive-free, waiting on my desk tomorrow morning. And another thing. The carriage cushions are filthy. Look at my gloves.' Her Majesty departed. 
 'Fuck,' said the footman, fishing out the book from where he had been told to hide it down the front of his breeches."

Community Average Rating: 4.17/5

Review 1 (rated 3/5): "Guess was over hyped. ENjoyable and interesting, but not as good as I had expected. The theological aspects were not as convincing as could be - though the society with 2 intellegent species definitely made for an interesting aspect."

Review 2 (rated 2/5): "** spoiler alert ** 
 This is basically a book about mans faith in God and what happens when this is pushed to the limits. The story is wrapped round a Jesuit space expedition to Alpha Centauri and a 'first encounter situation'. I guess overall the story was okay, but it's been done better. As with many books nowadays this would had more impact crystallized into a short story. A lot of the book is fluff that only points out the weaknesses, not the strengths. The author would have been much better off not trying to tell this as a science fiction story. 
 Most reviews point out how great the characterizations are. True, they were pretty good but very inconstant. At the beginning of the book the main characters are all brilliant and there doesn't seem to be anything they cannot do. (The idea of a small group of people equipping the first expedition to another star reminded me of E. E. Doc Smith's Skylark of Space, but that's another issue.) But later, when they get to the alien world, they make some unbelievably stupid mistakes. Even on my own planet I know not to eat strange things. On an alien planet they go right ahead and try it. They were not even smart enough to bring along some mice for testing. 
 Most of the really bad decisions were only there for a convenient way to move the plot in a certain direction. For me that's just bad writing. But the really killer of the book was the actual moment of first contact. The main Jesuit Priest uses slight of hand tricks to make it look to the aliens like he's making flowers appear out of thin air. Now why would he do that? A few chapters on there is some discussion that they don't want to mislead the aliens into believing they are gods or starting a cargo cult. Make your mind up! After that point I was glad that Sandoz got what he had coming to him. Perhaps that simple act of deception is why God punished him. 
 The science in this book was mostly nonsense. Even worse than bad it made statements about existing technology they anyone can look up and see is just plain false. For an academic writer like the author, this lack of research is just mind boggling and inexcusable. For example: She constantly refers to the Alpha Centauri system as having 3 suns, which is technically true, but the 3rd red dwarf star is 0.2 ly from the other two. That would make it appear as a bright star, not a red sun. The Jesuits accelerate an asteroid using a mass driver and the stated logic is 'the bigger the asteroid is, the more fuel they have'. Perhaps she should look up Newton's Laws. And they can also 'circle at 0.2g' using a mass driver... :) 
 There was a good underlying story but I was constantly taken out of it by eye rolling bad science, stupid character decisions and contrived coincidences. I know that in real life the Jesuits are considered the scholars and scientists of the papal world, but this book made them look like arrogant, ignorant idiots. 
 2 stars and I'm being VERY generous."

Review 3 (rated 1/5): "** spoiler alert **

I have gone to Jesuit schools for more than five years and love Ignatian theology, and the thought of Jesuits in space was too amusing to pass up. The alien species were a disappointment, which is pretty horrible for a sci-fi space book. Most of all, I could hardly figure out what "deep questions" this book was trying to discuss. I dunno. It was a strange and unfulfilling read."

Review 5 (rated 5/5): "One of the most moving and luminous books I've ever read. Full review is on my blog at: http://parlezmoiblog.blogspot.com/200..."

The plot of the book focuses on a Jesuit priest, Emilio Sandoz, who is the only survivor of a space exploration to find an alien species. The story jumps back and forth between the time spent on the planet and when he returns home and is reporting to his superiors. Emilio finds his faith severely tested when things go terribly wrong. You will read the whole book to find out what has happened to him and rest of the crew. 
 It took almost half of the book before I really got into the story. I almost gave up on it, and that is why I'm giving it only a three star rating. However, the writing is excellent, the characters are great, and once the story really got going I enjoyed it. Overall I'm giving it 3.5 stars."

Review 7 (rated 4/5): "This was a curious combination of sci-fi and religion. It doesn't reach any definite conclusions."

Review 8 (rated 5/5): "The Sparrow is amoving and philosophical science fiction novel. This tale of the people of Earth's first contact with an alien species has a different twist than typical alien encounter stories--- in this book the mission to the alien planet is not sponsored or undertaken by a space program, it is sponsored by the Vatican."

Review 1 of "Dead Ice (Anita Blake, Vampire Hunter, #24)" (rated 3/5): "This book was borrowed from my local Library. After reading the last LKH book, from the Merry series, I am beginning to think there comes a point when writing long-running series' when the author can get so caught up in re-hashing the prior books they lose the forward momentum in their current offering. Sadly this was a huge problem with her last book (the title I don't even remember anymore, sadly) and an annoyance with Dead Ice. With over 20 books in this series, it's pretty safe to assume the fans know the past plots and characters really well. This is one of the few authors I re-read, so the constant re-telling of the old story makes for more pages, but no story advancement-- We've been with you for two dozen books, Ms. Hamilton-- WE KNOW the ongoing story lines and the characters. I loved the return to animator roots, and the crazy challenges Anita had to deal with for her job- unfortunately, LKH has started to do the quick and tidy all-in-one-chapter-wrap ups of the police/animator threads, while endlessly drawing out the relational threads. I'd love to see more balance. In this book, there was a lot of emphasis on Anita's looks and self-image, which was fine, if not somewhat overdone. And the polyamorous aspects, while not as focused as some reviews led me to believe, seemed to be drawn out with no relevance to the current book (yes there will be more-- for all the pages, there was no real advancement of the ongoing relationship threads). Now we get to my peeve-- what the heck is going on with the editing? OMGoodness! The editor should be fired - the grammar was shoddy, and if I had a nickle for every time the word "that" was used, I'd be taking myself out for a surf and turf dinner. --- USER'S PAST REVIEWS ---
Review 1 of "The Marriage Plot" (rated 2/5): "** spoiler alert ** 
 This was another of those books that I wanted to like more than I did. I'm beginning to suspect that most contemporary fiction just may not be for me. The general coming-of-age concept is one with which anyone can identify and understand, especially when combined with "the marriage plot." I actually like Mitchell and Madeleine's stages of marriage age, because being around the "Stage Two" age, of course I notice the same patterns. It makes you wonder sometimes about marriage and how it comes about, which is a different story. 
 Or is it? After all, how does Madeleine and Leonard's marriage come about? Because they were in that stage, or because they were in love? In my opinion, it's because they were in anxious denial. Madeleine seems determined to believe that if she just keeps open-minded about mental illness and steady on the course, that will be enough to cure Leonard. He on the other hand, is a scientist who feels like science is failing him, understandably frustrated and anxious to get on with his life. What happens when obstinacy and panic fall in love? A rushed and ill-conceived marriage, which even poor Mitchell, soul-searching in India, can see coming. 
 Yet it's not the relationship woes, frustrating as they are, which make me feel unsatisfied about this story. Given the characters (whom I admit I didn't find easily relatable or likable), their conflicts are sadly true. I read one review which called the book "over-written," which it may be at times, but at others it can be nicely descriptive. 
 I think my main problem with this coming-of-age tale is that nobody comes of age. Nobody ends up anywhere. Nobody does anything. At the end of the novel, the three characters are in virtually exactly the same positions they were at the beginning. The sole exception is Madeleine, in that she finally knows (kind of) what she wants to do with herself. But considering that Madeleine has had virtually no personality for the majority of novel outside of being Leonard's caretaker*, I can't bring myself to feel more than just vaguely pleased for her. Most of that pleasure lies in the fact that I hope she can finally live some facet of her life now. 
 *This made me think multiple times of The Dive From Clausen's Pier, and that question, "What do we owe those whom we love?" Despite my weariness with Madeliene, she demonstrated the struggle with that question beautifully."

Review 2 of "Bossypants" (rated 4/5): "** spoiler alert ** 
 I may be one of the few, but I did not go into this book expecting it to be laugh-out-loud funny. I expected the "Tina Fey Story," a tale of a girl growing up and landing a gig on SNL, then her own TV show and a run for the Vice Presidency. I didn't even expect her to go too deeply in depth about that, considering how recent it was and how much she is probably sick of discussing it. I was pleasantly surprised to find that while the book wasn't hilarious, there were definitely moments where I laughed aloud to myself (and that's why I tend to read alone where nobody will give me funny looks). 
 I'm not going to lie. Tina Fey's book is not the most amazing book ever, nor is she the most amazing writer ever. But she can tell a good story, and that is where her book shines. The best chapters are usually those in which she just tells the story of what happens, and you can almost hear her voice narrating it in your mind. The few exceptions in my eyes were "Delaware County Summer Showtime!" which had a lot of good in it but maybe just too many messages to get across, and "Young Men's Christian Association" which started well but faded by the end of the chapter. In fact, any part where I felt that Fey was trying too hard faded for me quickly. 
 What readers are likely anticipating most when picking up Bossypantsis the story of "Sarah, Oprah, and Captain Hook." That actually was not my favorite part of the book, but it was a fascinating read to see how the odd coincidence that these two women looked similar blew up into this media party. Fey may be (understandably) biased about the situation, but her overall point about how women are treated in comedy, and how she and Palin ended up on two sides of the same unfair coin, is valid. That is my favorite part of the chapter, other than the awesome Oprah joke and the way Fey puts together a birthday party for her daughter in the midst of pandemonium. 
 The only thing I didn't particularly like about this chapter was its location in the book. The rest of the book seems to flow more or less chronologically, but from this chapter discussing her daughter's 3-year-old birthday party, she jumps back in time to breast-feeding. It's a little bit jarring in a book that more or less has shown good continuity up to that point, apart from side-jumps discussing weight or addressing Internet commentary. My complaints are minimal though, because I love how Fey discusses her family, her approach to motherhood, and of course, her prayer for her daughter. 
 Overall though, I most appreciated the ways in which this book discusses the way women are treated in Hollywood. Some of them are surprising where I suppose they shouldn't be; for instance, men passed over women's sketches not because they were women's sketches but because the men didn't understand them. Some are not surprising and frustrating; for instance, men passed over women playing parts because they thought the men would be funnier. 
 What's impressive (and inspiring) is the way Fey confronts these things in her book with more confidence and humor and a lot less sarcasm than I would have. She's right to do so, of course: it is her determination to ignore labels, limits, and criticisms that makes it possible for her to overcome them. It's advice and an example that would benefit all women trying to achieve a goal. And it's that message, hidden between stories of improvs and tales of Photoshop, that makes this a good read.* 
 *No pun was intended, but that really made me smile."

Review 4 of "You're Never Weird on the Internet" (rated 3/5): "** spoiler alert ** 
 I continue to develop my interest in memoirs, which is fun. I began this book as an audio book, but could not actually make it past the first chapter. This is no insult to Felicia Day, but I found that reading it in print helped me embrace it more. Not to mention, there are visual jokes within the book which I wouldn't have fully enjoyed in the audio version (though I may go back and listen now that I've finished). 
 Day leads the reader through the story of her unusual upbringing and education, but what is actually more fascinating is the twist the story takes after her college graduation (though Day's intelligence is incredibly interesting!). Instead of fully exploring her acting career, or even going into any depth about some of her most popular roles at all, she instead chooses to focus on the anxiety and depression that led her into addiction and threatened her success both as an actor and as an entrepreneur. While her descriptions aren't heavy or frightening, they make reference to real threats which anyone suffering anxiety or depression might feel. I almost wish she had gone into more detail, since some things were touched on lightly or lightened by jokes (some I appreciated, some I did not). However, I'm sure these topics were hard for her to share, so I'll simply appreciate the bravery it took to face them as she did. I wouldn't say this is my favorite memoir I've read, but I'm glad I did read it and there were definitely parts of it I found inspirational."

Review 5 of "Narcissus in Chains (Anita Blake, Vampire Hunter, #10)" (rated 2/5): "** spoiler alert ** 
 If I'm to be quite honest, plot-wise, this book probably deserves 3 or 4 stars. I was intrigued by the possibility that Anita might be a shapeshifter and what that would mean for her work, her relationships, and her future. I really liked the development of Nathaniel's character (thank goodness!)and I was totally intrigued by the new pard in town. 
 Plot-wise, I felt like the biggest flaws were the slow beginning and the complete lack of development of the bad guys and the new coalitions. After Gregory was healed, I honestly felt like the book was going to be over except for apparently more sex until Marco and the snakes burst into the kitchen (also, I don't like Marco as a name for a lion-man, but that's just me and beside the point). My reaction was something like, "Oh, I should still be worried about these people? They're still important?" I simply didn't take them seriously as a threat. Even finding out the truth about Orlando King was only vaguely interesting, as there wasn't enough time left in the book to make him anything more dangerous or intriguing. 
 So if the book was decent plot-wise, what am I going to complain about? That's right, the sex. And no, while I'm sure many would consider me a prude, I'm not against having sex in the Anita Blake novels. I'm not even against having multiple sex scenes in the Anita Blake novels. What I hated was the way they disrupted the structure of the book. 
 I read one such scene straight through, and then expected to continue with plot. Instead, sex scene after sex scene followed, and I ended up skimming through 100 pages or more. I just found it boring to read about the same thing happening multiple times over a good fifth of the book. It would be like reading about Anita arguing with Dolph for 100 pages without a break. It's interesting the first time, repetitive the second, and downright dull anytime after that if it's not broken up by significant plot development. I don't call getting out of the shower, picking up Jean Claude, and taking him home significant plot development. 
 Just to prove my point, I'll point out that the sex between Anita and Richard hit the mark perfectly. They went through several major emotional and impacting events, converse, and sleep together, which felt natural and even beautiful in a way. It had been a long time since I recall such comfort and happiness between them. Then Anita tries to feed off him and he balks, continuing the plot, albeit in a sad way if you're a Richard fan (I am and I'm not). 
 Now... now I am torn. I would like to know more about the wereleopards and how things turn out with Nathaniel and Micah and the shapeshifter coalition. I'd like to see Anita resolve her relationships with Dolph and Ronnie. I would really like to see more Larry and Edward, because their presences were sorely missed in this book (especially now that I know so much about Edward!). I just have heard often that the books begin going downhill from here, and I'm not sure I want to waste another day skimming through most of a book just to get the good parts from it. Also, the preview at the end of the book seems to indicate that the next novel is primarily about Jean Claude, Asher, and Belle Morte, and I honestly am not interested. Well, I'm interested in Asher. He's fascinating. What to do..."

Review 6 of "Gulp: Adventures on the Alimentary Canal" (rated 3/5): "** spoiler alert ** 
 I greatly enjoyed this book. It was a lot of fun, filled with interesting and amusing facts, and Roach's sense of humor is (as usual) amazingly hilarious. The levity and tangential stories did distract a bit from the route that Roach was trying to take, but I still got a kick out of it. Review 7 of "Wither (The Chemical Garden, #1)" (rated 3/5): "This book is the closest I've been to bailing on a book in a long time. There are world-building issues with the timing of these genetic experiments and the logic of a world where people can only live to 20 or 25 that really bothered me (not to mention the ickiness of children having children! Ugh!), and I got so hung up on it that when my library loan ran out, I basically shrugged. But I'd forgotten I'd put a renewal on the before even starting it, in hopes I'd have enough time to finish it, and so when it became available again weeks later it popped right back into my Kindle. So I persevered. 
 In the end, I found it quite engrossing, though I never did make my peace with the world-building issues. But I really liked Rhine as a protagonist and wanted to know if she'd make it out of the mansion in this book, or if Rowan would find his way to her. She made some foolish choices which bothered me, and I wish she'd just told Linden the truth, but a good protagonist overall. 
 I also particularly liked the way the novel really emphasized female friendships and the sisterhood that can develop. It was a unique aspect to this story that you don't often see in dystopian novels, even when the heroines have sisters. That aspect really appealed to me, and even though I found Cecily aggravating, I appreciated what the author was doing. 
 Honestly, I'll probably never come back and finish this series, but it was better than I'd have expected based on the beginning. 2.5 stars rounded up."

Review 8 of "Aristotle and Dante Discover the Secrets of the Universe (Aristotle and Dante Discover the Secrets of the Universe, #1)" (rated 4/5): "** spoiler alert ** 
 This book was so very moving. So moving, in fact, that I'm struggling to review it. I love how it's not just a young adult love story, or another story about a teen learning to handle his or her sexual orientation. It's really about these teens learning to handle their identity as people. They look at so many rules and standards, and how they meet them and how they don't: they're Mexican, but not Mexican enough because they don't like certain things from their culture. They're supposed to talk about all their feelings, because that's what the right and adult thing to do is, and yet their parents have many feelings and thoughts they don't share. It's a struggle to face these many standards, and these are things that continue as people become adults. I love that the author includes that in the trials that these boys have to face. 
 On top of that, I love that the boys are smart and good and respectful, despite these struggles. They are frustrated and angry, but that's not all they are. I found that heartening, and I really cared about them. I wanted them to be able to face their fears and have the hard talks. They had good parents (I LOVE that they have good parents!), and the author paints the parents as real people with struggles, as well as caring and devoted mothers and fathers. It was a lovely picture of friendship and family and love of all kinds."

Community Average Rating: 3.54/5

Review 1 (rated 2/5): "After ANNIHILATION--which I really enjoyed--AUTHORITY was a bit of a letdown. 
 In AUTHORITY, we shift from the jungles and mystery of Area X to the offices and politics of the Southern Reach. There's little to no action. Some parts were very compelling, like the interview portions with the biologist...but those were vastly over-shadowed by long dragging periods in which Control (the main protag) goes on a wild goose chase for information. There's misinformation and double-crosses. Layers are added to the enigma that is Area X. Answers are provided, however, in typical "Lost" fashion, they're answers that lead to more questions. I won't give spoilers. Just know that this definitely feels like an interim novel purely meant to get us to the final novel. That's what it felt like at least. 
 This, of course, is required reading if you're taking on the entire trilogy...but this installment was a definite labor. I flew threw ANNIHILATION in a matter of days. AUTHORITY took some effort."

Review 2 (rated 3/5): "Sustains and even improves upon the first book's creepiness quotient. Also introduces actual characters! But a bit of a lackluster/cliffhanger ending. Definitely in for the third, but this doesn't stand on its own as well as the first."

Review 3 (rated 1/5): "If volume one of the Southern Reach trilogy (Annihilation) brings to mind Patrick McGoohan's The Prisoner - no names just numbers or in this case occupations, volume two (Authority), continues the theme - Johnny Rivers' "Secret Agent Man" meets The Avengers (John Steed, Mrs. Peel, and "Mother"). 
 We know the date: 10 years in our future. The characters have names. The location is still unspecified but the dangling gray moss and the climate suggests somewhere along the Gulf Coast. Every description, every detail is calculated to project a decaying, stagnant environment in contrast to the pristine, flourishing conditions in Area X. None of the suspense in the first volume carries over to the second - all of the action is mundane, despite the author's attempts to suggest the unknowable. The creepy nature of the environment gives the sole color to the story - a monochromatic rainbow of grays. 
 Volume two, written in third person, shifts the perspective to agent John Rodriguez, new director of the Southern Reach. He prefers to go by Control, hiding behind a nickname instead of a job title. He's also a spy for a shadowy agency known only as Central, represented by an equally vague character called the Voice. Control entered the family business, so to speak, following in the footsteps of his grandfather and mother who is also his handler. He is marginally more sympathetic than the biologist, probably because we are privileged to experience his inner dialogue - almost without end. 
 Much of Control's thoughts seem random. Whether this is meant to reveal his character or represents the author's personal thoughts and observations isn't entirely clear. Some of the lines seem like non-sequiturs with lots of incomplete sentences, more than should be noticeable. After a while you have to ask if Control is a dim-wit. It dawns on the reader well before Control that the Voice is exercising hypnotic commands on him. Control's semi-stream-of-consciousness is probably intended to reinforce the sense of a man teetering on the edge of sanity. Too often they come across as lines that may have sounded clever in the author's head but miss the mark on paper. When the author disappears, leaving the character's voice clear and resonate, it works. Mostly it is like a radio signal fading in and out. 
 The administration of Southern Reach is the primary focus of the novel. The military has a part to play but over time its role has devolved into boring routine. After 30 years without real progress, the bureaucracy has reshaped the scientific investigation. The distinct difference between the 60's space-age, rigorously scientific approach has been supplanted by a bureaucratic, institutionalized, decadent, decaying organization. The surviving staff seems to have a collective malaise or shared delusion or fatalistic attitude toward a dead-end occupation. These odd characters are sufficiently well-drawn, Whitby, Cheney, Grace - they are believable, even recognizable as people we know or have met. The situation Control encounters is reminiscent of the business world - staff reductions, low morale, recent failures, and focus on process not product. The enumeration of the expeditions, which we learn is closer to 40 despite the latest being called the twelfth, is similar to how executives decide software releases should be named and for similar reasons. 
 Beyond the incomplete sentences, there are editing flaws like this one on page 218-9: "A lone great blue heron stood solemn and silent in the middle of the pond. Thunderclouds continued to gather, its feathers dull in the fading light." Really? Thunderclouds have feathers? 
 Why are there 3 volumes? Volume 1 is clearly prologue. Volume 2 is set-up and volume 3 must be the big finish. Volume 1 ended at the point when continuing would have made it tedious. Not so with volume 2. The meandering style is beyond wearing. Cutting volume 2 by a third would have improved the story while still permitting the author's stylistic and creative choices. A single novel 600 pages long should be enough to tell the complete tale. 
 Turning page after page, I attributed my concern to Control - wanting the story to mean something but afraid it did not. In spite of the spooky setting and the ominous portents of Area X, the novel describes a rather dull storyline where the oddities of a misplaced cell phone, a dead mouse and undying plant, rummaged desk drawers, and a murdered mosquito signal the 'unusual.' Will I read volume 3? I finished the "Dire Earth Cycle" so I can manage this one. My expectations are pretty low."

Review 4 (rated 2/5): "Could have easily been shortened by 100+ pages. Fairly boring."

Review 5 (rated 1/5): "Holy crap, this book was unbearable! I'm trying to think of something good to say about this book...and failing. It reminds me of an unholy blend of the final season of Lost, The Blair Witch Project, Cloverfield, The Office, and Waiting for Godot. Endless trivial descriptions of bureaucracy, oblique dead-end details, and an obstinate refusal to further the plot in any way, other than with fruitless clues. It seems that fans of Annihilation were enthralled by the ominous Lovcraftian horror of Area X and the unreliable narrator, but the real horror is the unreliable author who writes well and teases with no intention of delivering the goods. 
 I am a prodigious reader of SF&F, but I am not a fan of ambiguity or metaphor. I want a novel with compelling characters, fascinating world-building, and a propulsive storyline that makes we want to know more, but whatever Jeff VanderMeer was aiming for, it went straight over my head. This book smacks of Serious Literature Filled with Deep Meaning that Average Joes cannot possibly grasp. As I read for entertainment and to stimulate my imagination, I cannot go another step. I was hoping this book would provide some illumination of the events of Annihilation, but after getting to the 50% mark without the slightest clue, I cannot justify wasting any more precious reading time. People often say, just hang in there and the book will pay off at the end, but I would counter, why can't a story be interesting and exciting from the get-go? Is that too much to ask? Having read fairly widely, I'm pretty certain of what I will like or not, and this series is about as far from my tastes as I've encountered in a long time. My apologies to all the GR readers who loved this book, I respect your opinions and tastes and I hope you won't think less of me, but why torture myself anymore? I'm moving onto something else."

The plot was sparse and mostly consisted of office politics, meetings, interviews, tours, meal breaks, theorizing, phone conversations, and some hum-drum flashbacks to the protagonist's past. I guess this is what happens when the setting is an office building rather than a mysterious, Lovecraftian landscape. Occasionally there are some tidbits about Area X's history and origins, but we do not learn much more about it than in the first novel. 
 My main criticism is that VanderMeer gives far too much space to the settings. There are frequent, lengthy, opulent descriptions of boardrooms, offices, containment facilities, research labs, living rooms, kitchens, and bedrooms. If you took these out, I bet you'd loose 100 pages. VanderMeer also gives his characters -even ancillary ones- similar treatment. 
 Stylistically, many of his analogies and similes are over-the-top. Here's an example: "A spiraling thread gone astray that might or might not be made of something else entirely - not even as scrutable in its eccentricity as a house-squatter of a nail that stumbled around like a drunk." Sometimes, he clusters them together and it's very annoying. I wish he would have put more effort into creating compelling dialogue rather than in trying to impress us with his vocabulary and figurative language. On that note, the dialogue is rather contrived and insipid. 
 I think the purpose of this book is to set up the next and final novel. That may explain why it was such a lackluster follow-up to "Annihilation". I really hope VanderMeer takes us back into Area X in "Acceptance", because it is a far more interesting place to be."

Review 3 (rated 3/5): "Ready Player One is the most referential book I have ever read. Its pages drip with 80s pop culture references, some of them obvious, many of them not. It's entertaining at first, especially when you understand the reference, but then it becomes a bit obnoxious and excessive. This, in fact, is a good analogue to the book itself. Its beginning is much stronger than its conclusion, and the aspects of the book which were its most entertaining element at the start become tired and worn-out by the end. 
 The book is on the whole enjoyable. I described it to a co-worker as "aggressively okay." The narrative pulls you along at a steady pace, interesting things happen, the mystery of the "Easter Egg" is sufficiently compelling, but it's the finer details that start to nag. As mentioned, the references, the worship of 80s culture, although explained through the narrative, becomes irritating. The details of the story are impressive, and the author's passion for the subject matter screams on every page. The writing and dialogue serves the story fine and provides only a few moments of profundity. 
 Sadly, the author, Ernest Cline, commits one of the most grievous mistakes of any science fiction or fantasy story, which I call "The Magic Wand." Essentially "The Magic Wand" is a narrative tool to magically fix the story's most perplexing problems. (Did you know reversing the Earth's orbit reverses time itself!? Thank you, Superman). Often times authors use this Wand when they've painted themselves into a corner. "Oh, look, now the main character can fly!" or "travel through time!" or some such thing. Ready Player One's Magic Wand is the main character's outlandish sudden ability to perfectly plan and execute a plan of such devious and conniving genius it leaves both the characters in the book and the reader of the book completely stunned. Furthermore, throughout the book, there are far too many instances of the character needing to know some obscure or obtuse fact about 80s pop culture and the main character conveniently notifies the reader: "Good thing I've watched this film exactly 175 times." Good thing, indeed. 
 Having said all of this, I enjoyed Ready Player One for what it was. I was especially interested in the possible and entirely plausible future of virtual reality that the book showcases. It's both exciting and dismaying. Although the messaging of the book is muddled, which is too bad, the fiction aspect of it was very interesting. (It's worth mentioning that according to an article in Businessweek, each new Oculus Rift employee--a company which has created a virtual reality headset--is issued a copy of Ready Player One). A few years ago I was extremely skeptical of virtual reality's ability to be adopted by the mainstream. Although that hasn't happened in a significant way yet, I do believe it will; in addition, I believe it very well could herald a massive shift in how we consume and participate in entertainment, education, business, commerce, and even how we interact with and make sense of reality itself. Ready Player One shows a world that is either terrifying or exhilarating depending on your worldview. I'm not convinced the author knows exactly which one it is. 
 Ready Player One is being adapted into a film by Steven Spielberg, and I think it might have a better chance being a great story as a film than a book. I think the story needs to be trimmed, sliced and diced a bit, and leave behind many of the arcane details meant to be enjoyed by only a few. There is definitely a fun adventure to be found here, but it might take some other storytellers to tell it a bit better.

 1.5 stars Don't worry. That's the tame version. I didn't spoil the extreme parts of the story. Trust me. 
 It might be a long, long time before I read something which knocks American Psycho out of the top spot for "sickest thing I've ever witnessed," and I've read books which have had rape, murder, and gore aplenty in them. 
 How often can a person say that the movie was better than the book? I actually liked the movie because it carried the point from the story without being quite as tedious or gruesome. 
 Part of me wanted to spoiler-tag a couple of the more gruesome scenes, just to give readers who were curious something to look at. But I'm not giving anyone any ideas. O.o 
 The first half of the book was overworked satire. Pages and pages of excessive description gave no great sense of entertainment or enjoyment in terms of reading experience. I do understand why the author did what he needed to do in order to set up the character's state of mind to the reader. Many of the conversations and interactions were needed, and a few were actually informative or interesting, but the same point really could have been made in a few chapters. 
 It all comes down to reading preference for me. Half a book of recycled conversation about fashion, society, tanning, etc. is torture for people like me who could not give a shit about that stuff. I hate wasting my time by reading about stuff I don't want to read about, satire or not. Overkill is still overkill, especially when you see the same catch-phrases (hardbody, gazelleskin, etc.) used dozens of times in the book, and you're sort of sad that you're not playing a drinking game to combat some of the repetitiveness. By the time I got to the chapter on detailing Whitney Houston's career, I was downright tired of reading scene after scene of tedious information. 
 Although...the chapter on name brand water amused me, probably because of how I learned that I'm sparkling water poser. 
 Speaking of excessive...let's get to the second half of the book, otherwise known as a precursor (no, not really) to the show 1,000 Ways to Die. 
 Try thinking of the sickest way you could kill someone. Chances are, you aren't even close to thinking about what Pat put his victims through. 
 Did Pat become the way that he was because he was so rich and bored, and had nothing left to achieve or desire, or was his mind so completely ordered and methodical about everything from the start, that he viewed murder without emotion as just another thing he could organize and categorize? 
 I get why American Psycho has a good portion of its ratings on either one end or the other of the spectrum. Since the subject itself doesn't lend itself well to words such as "love" or "admire," a reader is either going to respect the method of writing, or hate the product of the writing. 
 I wanted to fall on the respect end because I understood why others rated the book high. But I can't overcome the fact that I hated reading the repetitive formula of : character talks about meaningless shit, character talks about or participates in unappealing (and super-extreme) sex, then character makes a gruesome kill. 
 The end of the story gave the reader nothing to wrap up the madness of it all. 
 The guy was a psycho. That's about it. At least the book was aptly named."

Did it blow me away, no, but this was a cute, quick story that was the perfect Christmastime read. I read this literally 2 days before Christmas, and it had everything that I wanted at that time...Christmas trees, pretty lights, hot cocoa, ugly sweaters, candy canes...I could go on and on! Honestly, I could easily see this being a Hallmark Christmas movie (and I'm a sucker for those things). The story was incredibly heartwarming and just a feel-good, light romance, and exactly what I needed.

I think that is probably true. 
 The basic plot is about two brothers who are 15 months apart and who begin life very close as most siblings that close in age might be. As one brother; Udayan grows up he becomes part of the Naxalite movement in India so the brothers grow apart. The other brother moves to America. The novel is in third person; however, the point of view changes between each of the characters to show how the events of the novel played out to each of them. The novel is one in which you get to stay with the characters for a long time so you get to see how decisions made affect future generations. 
 I hated the characters! I suppose that was the intention but for the most part each of them is wrapped up in their own life and make decisions without considering the others around them at all. The coldness of Subbash and Udayan's mother and Guari (Udayan's wife) especially make it hard to read without throwing your book or in this case my Kindle. Udayan's involvement in the Naxalite movement is what brings out my fury for politics in all its forms. Each side has their agenda, refuses to hear any other side or work out any kind of humane solution to problems. So the only thing that is accomplished is strife, and violence. 
 I did like the grand scope of the story because I like to know how the characters lives play out,maybe see just a little bit of a happily ever after for some of the characters. It gives you hope. The author does give us just a few rays of hope at the end.

Review 4 (rated 2/5): "http://www.hipsterbookclub.com/review... 
 In the memoir Committed: A Skeptic Makes Peace with Marriage, Elizabeth Gilbert approaches the topic of matrimony from a variety of angles: historical, sociological, psychological, and emotional. The idea behind the book holds promise, particularly in a time when marriage is scrutinized and on the cusp of evolution. Unfortunately, Gilbert never makes sense of all the facts and views she collects, and the book leaves the author confused and readers unfulfilled. 
 When the United States Department of Homeland Security denies her Brazilian lover and life partner access into the country, Gilbert must reexamine their relationship. Until that point, the two had maintained a fulfilling but unconventional relationship that satisfied their desire for companionship and independence. As survivors of painful and tedious divorces, the two had mutually rejected the concept of marriage altogether. In Gilbert's words, "We had sworn with all our hearts to never, ever, under any circumstances, marry." Faced with the choice of legal commitment or separation, they reluctantly agree to wed. 
 Playing off the momentum of her well-received 2006 book, Eat, Pray, Love, her latest account follows a similar formula. Anticipating the lengthy legal process before them and unable to be together in the United States, the couple travels through Australia and Southeast Asia. Gilbert capitalizes on this experience by interviewing women she meets in her travels on the topic of marriage, and she combines these first-hand accounts with research into the history of marriage as she attempts to make sense of a concept she wholly rejects. 
 One cannot fault the author for her skepticism. With outrageous divorce rates and the changing landscape of relationships, many question whether marriage is still an essential function of our culture. Historically, men and women took vows out of economic necessity or religious obligation. As Gilbert points out, today we benefit from more social, financial, and spiritual freedoms. Why, then, are we still choosing marriage? 
 Gilbert seeks not only clarity but also reassurance, claiming, "This entire book--every single page of it--has been an effort to search through the complex history of Western marriage until I could find some small place of comfort in there for myself." Fair enough. Where Gilbert struggles, however, is creating a story meaningful enough for an audience. 
 In fact, the author admits she wrote the book for 27 women in her life, including her stepdaughter, mother, and friends. She spends much of the book airing her views on companionship, marriage, and motherhood, much like one would vent frustrations to a close friend. More than once, she admittedly falls into rants. At times, her arguments produce thought-provoking and interesting points for the reader's consideration. A bride-to-be could benefit from contemplating a personal definition of marriage based on Gilbert's research of wedlock throughout history and cultures. However, many of the author's ramblings come off as self-indulgent tirades. 
 For example, Gilbert's diatribe on motherhood comes across as unbalanced and unnecessary. Though not a mother herself, she conveys the strain motherhood places on women. By divulging the personal sacrifices made by her mother and grandmother in the name of family, Gilbert resolves that an independent career woman like herself might better fill the role of "auntie." The entire section, though, feels like an excuse for Gilbert to justify her choice to remain childless and adds little to the overall discussion on matrimonial commitment: 
 I can see where I have been vital sometimes as a member of the Auntie Brigade... there are people I've been able to help, sometimes fully supporting them for years, because I am not obliged, as a mother would be obliged, to put all my energies and resources into the full-time rearing of a child... thereby freeing up resources to spread more widely across the community. In this way, I, too, foster life. 
 The lack of authority and reliability from the author detracts from the more interesting features of the book, such as the conversations with married women from different cultural backgrounds. She only scratches the surfaces with her interviews and then quickly drops the subject, as if she doesn't know how to process the information. Gilbert readily admits that she is not a "professional academic, nor a sociologist, nor a psychologist, nor an expert on marriage." The jumbled facts and figures presented throughout the book are interesting bits of trivia but also incomplete. For all her rants, interviews, and research, Gilbert achieves no clarity. She remains a skeptic until the end and concludes that marriage has changed throughout history and the dynamics of commitment differ between every couple. It required a journey throughout foreign lands and a year's worth of research to reach such an ironically noncommittal conclusion? 
 In Eat, Pray, Love, Gilbert inspired readers by emotionally connecting with them through her personal triumphs and losses. In Committed, her constant bellyaching and condescending attitude distance her from the audience and bury the smattering of noteworthy discourse. By the end of the book, readers will feel more sympathy for her patient husband than the confused and pessimistic Gilbert. Perhaps the book should have stayed between the 27 intended readers because it ultimately offers little wisdom or weight for an audience at large."

My main issue with the book is that at no point do any of the three main characters - Kirby, Dan, and Harper Curtis - ever become more than descriptions on the page. All three exist only insomuch as the author is telling you they do so: they don't become real or three dimensional in the mind of the reader, and neither does their world. The Harper character in particular was annoying because he never achieves any sort of depth: he's a serial killer like pretty much any other serial killer you've ever read about or seen on television. He does bad stuff just because. We know nothing about his background or anything about his life before or after his experience in the House that somehow just pushes him over the line from really bad guy to serial killer. The author offers up one scene that describes some minor animal torture and watching his brother get crushed under a tractor but again, it's par for the course for any serial killer and it offers nothing insightful about *this* particular serial killer. 
 At the start of the book, Harper is running away from a group of people out to do him some sort of harm but it's basically irrelevant in terms of learning anything about him. It's a very drawn out sequence of events, the purpose of which is just to get him to the House where he has this sensory experience while high on morphine that somehow just puts him on this path to hunting and killing the 'shining girls'. And that's about it for Harper in the character development front: he spends the rest of the book stalking and killing girls, and a few other people along the way because that's what serial killers do. At no point does he question what that transformative experience might have been about, or the very idea that this house is somehow a time traveling device/portal. He just immediately goes along with the entire situation. Alrighty, then. 
 Kirby isn't much better. She's a typical alternative/punky kind of girl who doesn't really fit in with mainstream society. Her history with the serial killer doesn't help matters but really, we're not offered much in the way of character development to know her better or sympathize with her much more than that. We get some scenes from her life as she grows up with her flakey, artistic mother Rachel. As an adult she's on the hunt for the man who tried to kill her but the sleuthing/mystery aspect of her story is woefully underdeveloped. Much like the characters in this story, the meat of the plot doesn't get much deeper than the page it's written on. Kirby doesn't really get far at all in terms of finding clues or making connections to Harper until near the end when the whole thing suddenly comes together for apparently no other reason than the author figured it was time to wrap things up. There's a really jarring chapter near the end where Kirby is in the House (which up to this point she didn't even know existed), hiding upstairs as she hears Harper (she doesn't know who he is then but knows he's the man who tried to kill her) coming in and up the stairs. This scene just pops up out of nowhere, and I actually flipped back a few pages to see if I missed something, or if this was supposed to be something she was dreaming about. No, it's just a weird prelude to later on near the end of the book when Kirby actually does find the House and goes inside. It was just a very strange choice structurally as the reader gets thrown right out of things. 
 Another small bit that frustrated me was an exchange near the end between Kirby and the police - she's pointed them to where Harper is living and having been in the House herself, she's seen how it's so different inside than out. Of course, the police go there and it's just a dilapidated abandoned house, inside and out. But when Kirby goes back, this time with Dan, and they both go in, Dan sees the House in the same way as Kirby and Harper: so why does it 'work' for him and not the police? Well, that's another cliche, isn't it? The protagonist tries to convince those in authority about her theory but they are unable to verify what she's said or what she's seen etc. So they think she's crazy and she has to go off to the scary house/location whatever and deal with it herself, thus triggering the final battle between plucky heroine and bad, evil man etc. etc. 
 I lost interest about half way through and just skimmed to the end. I figure if you haven't made the characters come alive and be more than descriptive words on the page by the halfway mark, then there's a problem. This book is big on its ideas but is woefully short on its ability to deliver."

Review 2 (rated 5/5): "This is an amazing story because even though the inspector figured out, over two other amateur professionals that all the suspects did it -- he also saw the foresight of allowing the train official decide to allow a willing suspect to take all the blame for the murder, as does all the other suspects. 
 This is a story that ties hope, courage, self-sacrifice and bravery with the authority being "wise" enough to cover up a sensational story and thus ruin the least amount of lives... because some criminals are that horrible. This is a world in which man -- not God decides what is correct. That even with technical accuracy and precise reasoning, man still decides to do: what is in his own self interest -- that all choices are a personal matter and not founded/justified on universality. 
 This is how the horrors and the sublime justices are one and the same: that power is bestowed by position and not by some universal good. This is a world where beauty and evil require that we forget one or the other, and in the end this is what is most shocking... Agatha Christie takes us to a deep place that is not easily left. In a sense the mystery unresolved through reasoning so clear, we see everyone's (except the dead's) point of view, so that the evil are the dead only because having all other points of view on the same page establishes what is real. That's how all the weak good guys need each other to defeat the evil bad guy. That's how ideology excludes one of us. That's how only acceptance is good, and the material body of the spirit is the consensus of those who count. 
 For us to be all spirit, we require an invisible reminder to be excluded. The evil marks the border of a transcendental bubble that contains only what can be accepted as being a certain way. This necessary nothing is what is required to establish the minor difference between differences. The question then becomes, what nothing is each nothing -- or are they all the same? Did society truly condemn this man to die, or is the authority afraid of this group? We shall never know. 
 This is a rich book that can be seen in a variety of ways. The solution to this mystery and its subsequent resolution crystalizes the relationships in a way that is undeniably true. In this sense, a mystery is a very detailed account of truth through pure reasoning, but only because the book ends, and then we cannot know everything or anything. We then know the limit of this reasoning, which is what the detective is supposed to find -- exploit and then present the deeper Truth which is reasoning.
