Each section is delimited by a header of the form --- SECTION NAME ---, marking the start of a new block of reviews. The user's past reviews are formatted as: Review {i} of "{title}" (rated {rating}/5): "{review_text}". Community reviews for each candidate book are formatted as: Review {i} (rated {rating}/5): "{review_text}".

--- USER'S PAST REVIEWS ---
Review 1 of "This Savage Song (Monsters of Verity, #1)" (rated 5/5): "Can't wait for #2!! A bit dark, pretty action packed, solid cast of characters"

Review 2 of "Vassa in the Night" (rated 2/5): "The window to this world wasn't open quite enough for me to be pulled in. I could see it as a good school book though, especially with the guide in the back."

Review 3 of "Kushiel's Dart (Phèdre's Trilogy, #1)" (rated 3/5): "Had some problems keeping track of all the minor characters... Then I finished the book and found a dramatis personae section."

Review 4 of "Three Dark Crowns (Three Dark Crowns, #1)" (rated 2/5): "I had a really hard time getting into this. Way too much romance drama. Not much else. Little character development, not much plot until the end. I didn't realize it was a series and was looking forward to a resolution but got mad when there wasn't one. Couple of decent twists though. In the last... 25 pages? I don't actually know. It was a lot to get through to get there though."

--- COMMUNITY REVIEWS FOR BOOK A: "The Rithmatist (Rithmatist, #1)" ---
Community Average Rating: 4.25/5

Review 1 (rated 1/5): "Sorry, Brandon Sanderson -- I've loved everything else of yours that I've read, but this one couldn't even inspire me to finish it. 
 And that's despite the fact that it's a middle-grade* novel that would only take a couple hours of dedicated reading to get through. 
 The characters are all flat and predictable -- naively enthused protagonist, endearingly-cluttered professor mentor, irritable and artsy female foil, snidely aloof professor red herring, militant investigator... Not a one is all that memorable. The mystery element might be intriguing, if readers had any reason at all to care about the Rithmatists-in-training who have been killed, or about any of those at risk of being targeted next, but none of them is shown in any detail. Our protagonist, in fact, is notable mainly because he doesn't fit the killer's profile -- not very conducive to raising the tension. 
 The one highlight of the book is, as in so many of Sanderson's books, the worldbuilding. Both the altered history and the magic system have heaps of intriguing potential -- but not nearly enough to get me to keep reading when none of the other elements inspire anything but yawns. 
 So I'm throwing in the towel. One star, and I'm clearing it from my currently-reading shelf. Better luck next time. 
 *I consider this book middle-grade, despite its marketing as YA, because there's really nothing even remotely teenagerly about it -- no hormones, no feel of being on the brink of adulthood. Without any of those themes, there's no reason for it to be any less appropriate for a ten-year-old than for a member of the supposedly-intended age group."

Review 2 (rated 2/5): "This is the first Brandon Sanderson book that I have not loved. I'm disappointed I can't give it five stars, but in all honesty, I can't. The magic system (while supremely well-thought-out as always) is kinda...boring, the characters are two-dimensional, and the 'steampunk' is limited to an off-hand mention of a few clockwork pieces. It's perilously close to 'gluing a few few gears on it'. 
 That said, I *am* intrigued by the mentions of the Tower, and its contents, so perhaps I'll pick up the sequel and give this series a second chance. Just because it's Brandon Sanderson. If it were anyone else, I wouldn't have even finished the first book."

Review 3 (rated 4/5): "Every time I read one of Brandon Sanderson's books I'm in awe of the man's imagination. He always comes up with unique and interesting systems of magic, and then injects so much detail into them you can't help but be sucked in. The Rithmatist is no exception. The magic is based on chalk drawings, and so it all takes place in two dimensions. It seems silly and like there's no way it could work, but it does. I look forward to the next in the series."

Review 4 (rated 3/5): "3.5. Interesting and good beginning to a new YA magic series. Harry Potter-like but different, thankfully not a lot of love interest or clunky exposition."

Review 5 (rated 5/5): "Who would have thought that geometry and chalk drawings would provide some of the most interesting and intense storytelling? Brandon Sanderson creates a world where drawing figures made of chalk can create some of the most terrifying monsters. I was dubious about the premise at first, but I was soon won over. The heroic battles had me on the edge of my seat as I became engrossed in the theory and practical application of the "chalklings". The characters are very well-rounded, the story is interesting, the magic system is ingenuous and detailed, and the writing is brilliant! This book completely sucked me in and I cannot wait to read the rest of the series. You'll never look at chalk drawings the same way again!"

Review 6 (rated 5/5): "This book towards the middle and end started to get quite a mystery, crime, and thriller novel feel to it with fantasy aspects still mixed in. I loved this about the book. There were points were I would get nervous or scared because of the shocking events unraveling before me. The characters were very easy to relate to and the character development in this book was very well done. I could never have guessed how the book would end, but I know now that the ending was amazing and that I am ready for a sequel."

Review 7 (rated 5/5): "Really good, quick read. Took me about 3 hours to finish. Not up to Sanderson's usual standard of worldbuilding, but really good for a YA book. Plot was great and magic system was really fun. Hoping there'll be more to the series eventually. Whenever he gets around to it lol."

Review 8 (rated 4/5): "If Brandon Sanderson can keep up with all the series he's started, we have a lot to look forward to -- beginning with "The Rithmatist" (Tor, $17.99, 368 pages). 
 Be warned, however, that "The Rithmatist" is cast as a young adult series, and features teens as the lead characters. This is a departure for Sanderson, though not necessarily unwelcome, but another departure is the slow pace. As usual, Sanderson has crafted a detailed magical system on an alternate earth (the United States is a collection of islands rather than a continent), but it takes a while for all the parts to engage. 
 There are also a few holes in the plot (the villain seems curiously uninterested in getting rid of his enemies at book's end), but given Sanderson's past work, I expect all will be explained moving forward. And speaking of moving forward, I also hope the series will pick up the pace now that the groundwork has been laid - and young adult category or no, Sanderson fans will find plenty to like in "The Rithmatist.""

--- COMMUNITY REVIEWS FOR BOOK B: "Soulless (Parasol Protectorate, #1)" ---
Community Average Rating: 3.91/5

Review 1 (rated 4/5): "Very interesting. Love the humor. Love the world building. Already started the second in the series. I am surprised I like Steampunk, but I said the same thing about vampires and werewolves."

Review 2 (rated 1/5): "Not something I could get into at all. It seemed "stereotypically unconventional" if that makes any sense. Like the author was trying way too hard at being eccentric. Felt really forced and unbelievable."

Review 3 (rated 3/5): "Soulless was picked as the book for hour book club but I've been wanting to read it for some time before that. 
 It starts out exciting but sometimes the book got really boring and I have to admit that I didn't understand all the British words. But I loved them anyway. 
 The love story was more fun than the crime story, especially since I've figured out one of the culprits when he was introduced so that definitely took out some of the surprise. 
 Alexia Tarabotti was a strong female character and I enjoyed reading about her. I don't know why it was necessary to mention so often that she's part Italian but oh well."

Review 4 (rated 4/5): "A nice steampunk/urban fantasy/romance that's a bit of fluff, but still pretty entertaining. 
 --Leisa"

Review 5 (rated 3/5): "Much fun"

Review 6 (rated 4/5): "This was unexpectedly funny. I grinned so hard at the lisps (if you know, you know). Liked the character and all the nuances of her position in society. And her personality! Definitely going to pick up the sequel. Very entertaining. I mean, who doesn't like steampunky parasol-wielding ladies?"

Review 7 (rated 4/5): "It admittedly took me a few chapters to really be able to get into this book. The descriptions of society, coupled with the point of view were at first, too overwhelming and distracting. It just took a little adjusting before I felt truly comfortable and into the story. 
 But once I did, I literally finished this book in a week and couldn't stop reading. The humor and wit used throughout had me rolling with laughter and I ultimately fell in love with Alexia, Lord Maccon and above all, Lord Akeldama. I adore that Alexia is a woman of strong opinions and unlike other female characters, she can hold her own against any man. A genuinely unique idea here and I love what Gail has done combining them all. 
 I will definitely continue this series! Kudos to Carriger on this one...she had me on board by the end."

Review 8 (rated 4/5): "I enjoyed this book a lot. I am not sure I thought it was as great as everyone else but it was fun. I will have a full review up soon."

--- COMMUNITY REVIEWS FOR BOOK A: "The Promise of Amazing" ---
Community Average Rating: 3.50/5

Review 1 (rated 1/5): "Couldn't finish it. The non-meetcute and empty characters were just too much. Too cliche, too insufferable and a non-existent plot. I made it about halfway through. Nope. 
 Also, why is stalking only okay when the guy is hot"

Review 2 (rated 1/5): "I could not finish this book. 
 Three words: InstafreakingLove"

Review 3 (rated 2/5): "2.5 Stars; 
 Unfortunately this book did not live up to its title. Rather than getting the promised amazing, I just sorta got mediocre. On a really good day when I only read the parts I like it might be 3 stars. It had a lot of potentially but I felt like the story kind of lost itself and I just didn't know what was happening anymore. 
 I was expecting a cute highschool romance between two unsuspected teens. Wren is very quiet. She just doesn't like to talk. But because of that she's often overlooked and so she decides that's going to start changing. Grayson was a very interesting mixed character for me. He seemed like the both the all-American boy, with good looks, pretty good grades and athletic and the total bad-boy, the "male slut" (as he called himself) with no regards for others. And currently, he's kind of going through a mid(teen) life crisis. 
 At first, the story started off well. They had an awkward introduction, followed by some cute moments, and I was doing good. Than it got a little weird. Suddenly it was dive off the deep end instalove, with this crazy plot of an evil ex-best friend, and I just lost focus of what was happening. Is this a love story? Is this a self-discovery story? Is this a story about blackmailing & black marketing stolen stuff? The answer is: all the above and none of the above (are you confused yet? Because I was.). I think this book was trying to be too much and ended up with a multiple personality disorder. Point it, I didn't connect at allll with either Wren or Gray. Sure, I was happy they found each other, but I didn't care. The second half the book seem so entirely irrelevant to everything, or maybe I gave up by then, I don't know. I was just so confused. 
 I wanted to like the book. So here's a quick list of the stuff I did like: 
 1. Some sweet and funny moments (which is where the 3 stars came from) 
 "No, it's a date. I said, trying to tame my lame-ass grin. "I'm taking her ice skating." 
 "Skating? How retro," Tiffany said. 
 "Not retro. Perfect. Movies are a gamble. Dinner breaks the bank. When you skate you can hold hands without looking like you want more. And, well, if she falls, you can help her up, be the hero." 
 -see? Cute. 
 2. The cover and title 
 3. The name Grayson 
 But overall, the book fell flat to its moniker and didn't deliver. 
 {* Thanks to the publisher & Edelweiss for providing an eARC copy of this book in exchange for an honest review. Original review @ Book Munchies"

Review 4 (rated 1/5): "This book did not live up to its title."

Review 5 (rated 3/5): "3.5 stars. 
 This book is an ordinary teenager love story that reminds me of something you'd catch on ABC Family while flipping channels. 
 Wren is a girl who is stronger and more complicated than she appears. Grayson's a guy with more depth than he's been showing the world. 
 They fall in love quickly and drama ensues. 
 It was entertaining and I liked it. It just wasn't extraordinary."

Review 6 (rated 4/5): "3.5 stars! Review to come!"

Review 7 (rated 3/5): "3.5 
 This was really cute and I enjoyed it. A bit of insta-love, but not to an awful degree."

Review 8 (rated 2/5): "I didn't have much sympathy for Grayson-the way he manipulated and hurt people was just wrong, and no matter how you slice it, is a major flaw in his character. I don't think it's healthy or realistic that he wanted to change his whole life around just because of a girl, even though he was kind of on the right track to fixing himself up. The chemistry between the two main characters was nothing to write home about and their instantly fulfilling relationship was not in any way realistic. Also, way too much obsessing over looks- and in a general "he's so hot" way, which just pained me to read over and over. This book was way too long and, though I doubt this what the author had in mind when titling the book, I'm pretty "amazed" that I made it through the whole thing."

--- COMMUNITY REVIEWS FOR BOOK B: "Everneath (Everneath, #1)" ---
Community Average Rating: 3.76/5

Review 1 (rated 4/5): "I don't really know why I liked this book so much, but I really enjoyed it! I think maybe it was a combination of a few things: 
 -Every time Nikki started to get whiny, she stopped. 
 -Even though she blamed Cole for what happened, she also took responsibility for her actions in it. 
 -I'm quite partial to stories where the first guy {ie- boyfriend, long time best friend, guy with a forever crush on the girl} gets the girl. Pleasantly happy when the paranormal new guy doesn't get the girl, and I think that's what will happen here. I hope."

Review 2 (rated 2/5): "The writing was fine, and the world even better, but felt no connection towards the characters at all. I really wanted to like this book but by the end I just wanted it to be over. I wanted to care about the characters, to care if they lived or died, but I just didn't. Sad. The cover's pretty though."

Review 3 (rated 5/5): "This book is stunningly beautiful.From the writing and characters to the flawless blending of myth and reality, it is perfect. Not to mention the gorgeous cover, I mean, really, what girl doesn't dream of a dress like that? 
 What caught me most was the writing. It was dramatic and completely character-centric. No unnecessary words or long, rambling paragraphs. Yet it never felt rushed and flowed naturally throughout. I loved how the author managed to portray such intense emotions with such subtlety. I also truly love what she did with two of my favorite myths, Orpheus and Eurydics and Hades and Persephone. 
 Nikki is wonderful. She's so quiet that you don't always notice, but she has a will of steel. Knowing that she has little time before she is lost to torment and death, her greatest wish is to make it easier on the people she leaves behind. Especially for Jack. 
 Ah, Jack. My favorite character. He's a really, really nice guy with hints of a rebel that sneak out with an eyebrow piercing. He doesn't know where Nikki has been for so long, but he knows that she's been hurt. So he is what she needs most; a friend. He never pushes too hard, but he never gives up. He may take a step back at certain revelations, but never for more than a moment. 
 Cole is an entirely different kettle of fish. He's dark through and through, and has undoubtedly done terrible things, but is he completely irredeemable? Perhaps, perhaps not. It should be...interesting. 
 I would recommend this book to just about anyone, but especially lovers of mythology and beautiful, beautiful romance. And to people who don't mind shedding a few tears over a magnificent ending. 
 I received an advance copy of this book through the author in exchange for a fair and honest review."

Review 4 (rated 1/5): "This is a textbook example of a book that is not necessarily terrible, just terrible for me. I gave it 10 pages."

Review 5 (rated 4/5): "4,5 stars 
 I'll be strictly honest here: The first and main reason why I own this book is it's georgeus cover. 
 When I first opened account here on goodreads, back in 2013, I couldn't help but notice it and a material girl in me wanted to have it on her shelf. 
 Only recently I learned that Everneath is a reteling of a greek myth about Persephone. 
 You have my premission to judge me! 
 In the first few chapters I was little afraid this would be one of those ya books that have so many similarities with Twilight. I was little annoyed how Nikki went in Return and all she was thinking about was Jack. The main reason why that annoyed me was that she didn't spend that much time with her brother and dad. She claimed she wanted to spend her last days in Return with people she loved, but it seemed to me that for a first few months she spend them alone. 
 I know her dad was busy and had elections, so that explains his absence, but why there was no more scenes with her little brother? 
 I had a feeling that in the first half of the book we only get to know about him when Cole mentions him, and Nikki's afraid Cole would hurt him, but we don't get actual scenes with Nikki and little Tommy. 
 After I got over that I actually started to enjoy the story. 
 Nikki was an okay main character. She wasn't Mary Sue most of time. She was very slefless and that sometimes got on my nerves. 
 At first I wasn't a fan of Jack but somewhere in the third third of the story I fell for him. I am Team Jack all the way! 
 Cole was an interesting charater but I never precieved him as a love interest. Despise that, I'm looking forward to read more about him. 
 I never paid much attention to Jules. She was just there. I know she had a reason to be in the story, but I didn't feel interested enough to connect with her. 
 The most ineresting person in this book was Meredith. 
 The writing style in not unique but it is not as ussual eather. 
 As we read we go back and forward from past to present. 
 It is also beautiful and I found some noteworthy quotes that I underlined in my copy of the book. 
 Overall, I had a good time reading this book and I will gladly continue with the series. 
 My reaction right after finishing the book: 
 I can't believe I read this book in a day! 
 I guess that's what happens when the book is good!"

Review 6 (rated 1/5): "What worked: 
 Greek Mythology is a one way ticket to Fangirl Kingdom. It's not like I know a lot about the different myths and legends but there's something about them that I just can't get enough of. Brodi Ashton's new twist on the Persephone myth (which is something I've read a LOT of) is very intriguing and I liked the hierarchy of the Greek system. 
 What irked: 
 Have I been reading the same book as everybody else? My good friend, Brooke, really enjoyed it and normally our taste in books is spot on but with Everneath it wasn't happening. I actually did a buddy read with Hollie from Music, Books and Tea and the only thing that kept me sane is that she felt the same way about it. Everything about it was a disappointment. 
 Nikki is so frustrating and drab in a way that reminded me of Bella Swann. The whole reason she fought so hard to come back home was so she could put things right when actually she spends her time ignoring issues and focusing on the stupidest of tasks instead of the people she cares about. She jumps to conclusions and as for her pathetic excuse for going to the Everneath with Cole, don't get me started. I don't even see the appeal for this leading man. He's boring, he's kinda obsessive and he's a bit creepy and as for the other part of the "love triangle", I'm reserving judgement on Jack for now. He's a forgettable character to me and actually I have a question. Nikki creeps into his room at night (because obviously some YA characters have a blindspot for the creep factor) and he puts on some glasses. Hold on, did he already have glasses? Does he wear contacts the rest of the time? Because right now the image in my head is changing drastically with this sudden piece of information. Before she'd even climbed through his window I was already wondering about the logistics of it because Nikki looks through his window. It's 2am people, does he have blinds? Does he have curtains? If so, why aren't they CLOSED?! If I had a bedroom on the ground floor at the front of the house, I'd be gripping onto every bit of privacy I could, especially with riff raff clambering through my window when I'm sleeping."

Review 7 (rated 3/5): "3.5 
 Really it was just what I expected it to be: a little mindless entertainment. It was pretty well done for its kind - not too many annoyances and pet peeves - but it does stick to a typical romance and "special" girl who always thought she was normal storyline."

Review 8 (rated 1/5): "Just found the worst, dumbest, most passive protagonist in the history of literature. Absolute shit. Love triangle with most-popular-boy-in-school quarterback and handsome rock god demon... kill me."

Review 1 of "Alienated (Alienated, #1)" (rated 1/5): "Review also on: http://sonichreads.tumblr.com/post/16... 
 What fucking purpose does this book serve? Nothing! 
 Seeing the cover from afar, I thought it looked great. Really interesting choice of vibrant colors. Up close, good fucking bye. The cover looks shitty. And not to mention how boring it was, it was straight up 1-star since the beginning. I was so pissed off to the point where I wanted to DNF this book so much, but the thought of having its sequel already stopped me (and also, waiting to rant about it). I have a lot to complain about this book, and let me tell you. 
 "Curling one hand around his neck, she pulled him down, expecting a slow kiss. Instead his mouth came hard against her and melted her bones." 
 God, I'm hyperventilating. 
 1. Writing: Really, this type of writing style doesn't attract anything. It pushes it away. I couldn't find this either attractive or captivating. It was entirely boring. Its inability to grip me since the beginning turned me off already and that's one of the reasons why I wanted to DNF this book. I wasn't hooked to the book and I wished to finish this book as fast as possible because I didn't want to deal with it. It was purely disgusting with the choice of words used to describe what the characters were doing. It may seem metaphorical, but it is not. If you're looking for a poetic, well-composed, and beautiful writing, find The Wrath & the Dawn. 
 2. Genre: Do I need to be reminded again what genre this book is? I was quite clear it was sci-fi. And now it didn't give me the fucking sci-fi book I had expected. This book is a stupid and horrendous example of YA fiction. It showed a planet, which name is L'eihr, that's for aliens. Okay, the planet was exactly like Earth, aliens looked like humans; there wasn't any differences and they had their stupid negotiation and emails could be sent within the matter of short time. That's so fucking unique and special and original, Melissa Landers. 
 3. Plot: I had been expecting so so so much from it, that there would be plot that would blow me away and there wasn't, that's why this book is a piece of shit. Cara and Aelyx going to school, that's it, end of Alienated. I was unable to drag myself into the book again once I put it down because it was that boring.  The books get worse, it's like drinking alcohol, one or two books is ok. But by the time you get to the third book, you may feel nauseous. 
 Phill Pullman reminds me of a long winded Jedi: "these are not the droids you are looking for." weaving a reality distortion field around his story. Where the ultimate message isn't just that there isn't a God, but that it's limiting to believe in God. 
 A quote from Terry Pratchet's, The Hogfather : 
 Death: Humans need fantasy to *be* human. To be the place where the falling angel meets the rising ape. 
 Susan: With tooth fairies? Hogfathers? 
 Death: Yes. As practice, you have to start out learning to believe the little lies. 
 Susan: So we can believe the big ones? 
 Death: Yes. Justice, mercy, duty. That sort of thing. 
 Susan: They're not the same at all. 
 Death: You think so? Then take the universe and grind it down to the finest powder, and sieve it through the finest sieve, and then show me one atom of justice, one molecule of mercy. And yet, you try to act as if there is some ideal order in the world. As if there is some, some rightness in the universe, by which it may be judged. 
 Susan: But people have got to believe that, or what's the point? 
 Death: You need to believe in things that aren't true. How else can they become?"

Review 2 (rated 1/5): ""Love you Forever." Or more ACCURATELY, "Love You for a Limited Time Because I Am Going to Die." 
 "I love you forever...As long as I'm living, my baby you will be (or your mommy I will be)." 
 This line, or something close to this, is repeated on every page. This phrasing sounds to me like it REALLY SAYS, "I will love you forever. . . Well, not REALLY FOREVER but at least until I die. Until I die I will love you and we will be baby and momma and I WISH it was forever but I WILL DIE so our love and our close relationship WILL END. But until then I love you SO much." 
 The story line reinforces this showing a timeline beginning with a young mother singing this to her son throughout his life. Eventually the son grows up and lives in his own house with his own baby. At the end the mother is elderly. The son drives to his elderly mom's house, creeping into her room and singing a version of the song to his mom. I don't remember the exact words and can't look it up because I hid my copy at the top of my bookshelf so that my kids don't ask me to read it to them. The language is there, of course, referring to someone's "as long as I'm living" finite life period. In the context of his visit to his mother I find it implied that she is dying or it is a reminder that she is old and will die. After that, the man goes home and sings the song to his baby. 
 To me, this story portrays a heartbreaking love between parent and child. EVERY TIME this deep love and parent-child love relationship is mentioned there is always the limiting condition that this love and bond lasts for a finite time period, "as long as I'm living." 
 This book triggers DEEP feelings of sadness in me and causes me to think about dying and leaving my kids motherless and of losing my loved ones to death. Death is the final and permanent separation between all loved ones and lasts much longer than our brief lives on this earth. 
 ***** 
 Every time I've tried to read it to a kid I end up bawling and the kid ends up crying too. Actually, every time I've read it to anyone I cry and the other person usually starts crying, too. 
 I read it to my spouse. "Look how sad this book is! Let me read it to you!" I said. As I read, tears started STREAMING down my face. Seeing me look so heartbroken caused my stoic spouse to cry and he asked me to please stop reading it. 
 The BIG problem with the book is this. The refrain, repeated on every page, goes something like this, "As Long as I'm Living...my baby you will be (or your mommy I'll be?)." It doesn't really matter about the second part of the phrase, the loving sentiment, because it is conditional on the first part..."As Long As I'm Living...." 
 ***** 
 I love my kids. I don't tell them, "I love you so much but every time BEFORE I tell you this I MUST POINT OUT: THIS LOVE WILL EXPIRE! This loving feeling and our familial relationship is a LIMITED TIME OFFER. GET IT WHILE IT'S HOT!" 
 Every time "As Long As I'm Living. . ." is chanted I hear the corollary "I may be alive now but I AM going to die. As guaranteed as my love for you, so is my death." Worse yet, "You won't be my baby and I won't by your mommy. And I feel I must remind you of this every time I repeat this line and every time we read this book." 
 Most kids are terrified of death and become scared at the thought of being temporarily separated from their parents and are even more scared by the concept of a parent's death. Some kids may hear this words and not hear the implied "death" concept but I promise you SOME KIDS WILL. I do not recommend this book as a gift for ANYONE. Unless, of course, your goal is to emphasize the finite duration of love and relationship between close family members. In that case, this book would be most appropriate. 
 As a kid I would hear this message: "Sorry kids, life really sucks and we're all gonna die. Don't worry I will PROBABLY die before you. If you grow up to become parents one day YOU will probably die before your KIDS do . . . Of course, when you kiddos are parents your kids COULD DIE before you do and YOU KIDDOS could bite the dust before me! Don't worry about that for now. You and I have no control over my or your death. It could happen at any time. So don't worry about it. At least know that I'll love you and stick around as your parent for as long as I can...As long as I'm living! Again, I have little control over the duration of that period. But UNTIL the day of my or your sudden death . . . WE ARE GOLDEN!" 
 I would prefer the words "Forever and ever . . ." "Forever and Ever Your Mommy I Will Be, Forever and Ever My Baby You Will Be." I will always be my child's parent. My parents will always be my parents and I will be their child even after they are no longer on this earth with me. They are irreplaceable. Their love for me goes with me wherever I go. 
 Likewise, I try to instill into my kids the gift of love and belonging. I want them to know I love them now and forever. In my heart I am and will always be their mother and they will always be my babies even when they are grown up. I will love them every day of my life and beyond if that were possible. 
 I share with my kids that my grandparents live on in my heart and in my memories of their lives and of their love for my parents, me and for them. My elders have passed down so much love and knowledge and my children will do the same for their loved one. For me, this is forever love, or at least a love that continues beyond death and THIS is a truer way to teach kids and loved ones that we love them forever."

Rowling such a fan or Rowell that she didn't bother picking up the phone to slam her with a copyright lawsuit? 
 I admit, I haven't read Fangirl. Maybe if I did, this book would make more sense. But, as it is, I just felt wrong reading this amateur copy. Not only would it make more sense if she had actually written a few more books to give us a better understanding of Simon's journey, but the love story pre-kissing was just non existent. It actually sounded like any fanfiction where Harry and Draco end up together when there's NO build-up for a romantic relationship in the original world. I get the Harry/Draco thing, cause I used to be a big fan of them together (still am a little, reincarnated in a Scorpius/Albus fan). But J.K. never even hinted at a romantic link between those two. And that's how Rowell wrote Simon. No romantic attraction AT ALL. Until the big kiss that just comes out of nowhere... and made no sense... 
 Also, who the hell uses the F-word every few pages? I get that your characters are teenagers, but nobody thinks or says the F-bomb that many times... And don't get me started on the parenthesis...

Review 6 of "Girl Online (Girl Online, #1)" (rated 4/5): "UPDATE: I have been made aware that the book was actually written by a ghostwriter. Since Zoe Sugg came up with the idea, some of the praise still go to her. But it is obvious that any praise on how the story was written go to the ghostwriter. 
 Despite its cliches and lack of diversity, I quite liked this book. 
 The story is quite simple: a girl who seems unable not to make a fool of herself at every turn - and who runs a popular anonymous blog - goes on a trip to New York with her family. There, she meets a really hot guy and a romance sparkles between the two. A perfect Cinderella story, until she learns his secret. Everything resolves itself in the last 10 pages. 
 Famous blogger Zoella took a love story that has been used too many times and found a way to make it appealing to 21st century teens. Penny blogs, has Facebook/Twitter/Instagram, goes viral on YouTube at one point, is subject to fangirls' wrath online... All those are things teens and young adults of the 2010s have seen and done. And there are lessons hidden in all Penny's misadventures. Take her "reveal" by CelebWatch, for example. The 2 lessons hidden there are 1)don't believe the gossips and 2)don't bully girls on the internet because they are in the mere vicinity of your idol (or because they are rumoured to go out with your idol's rumoured boyfriend). 
 My only major problem with the story was that Penny's best friend Elliot is a bit too stereotypically gay. His journey (the parents problems, mostly) redeems him to a certain extend, but there are moments where his gayness becomes caricature. The description of his taste in clothes made me cringe at times. For all the other good things Zoe Sugg brought to her books, the gay-best-friend was far less well executed than the others."

Review 7 of "Simon vs. the Homo Sapiens Agenda" (rated 5/5): "Loved it!

Simon's friends and family are very accepting and, while not everyone is that lucky, it's a beautiful novel about coming out when you're a teen and so many things happen at once in your life. 
 The ending left me with a huge smile on my face, much like those very cliche romance novels sometimes do when they are well written. I was definitely rooting for Jacques and Blue."

Review 8 of "Rivers of London (Peter Grant, #1)" (rated 3/5): "3.5 [?] 
 FINALLY! It took me two weeks to finish this book, but I DID IT!! I usually read mostly while commuting, but being stuck at home all week since I've got back in the country, it was hard to do so. But the lack of commuting hours is not the only reason it took me so long to finish this book. I gave it 3 stars because it wasn't bad, but it wasn't amazing either. 
 When I read a murder mystery - even a supernatural one - I want it to be a page turner. I want to be out of breath while reading, eager to know what happens next and how they'll catch the murderer. The problem with this novel is that there is too much description. While it's interesting to learn about Aaronovitch's world of magic and the science behind it (my scientific mind loved it), most of the novel was focused on detailed description. A good part of those could have been less detailed and it wouldn't have taken anything from the novel. A moment that should have been quite important (Peter discovering Lesley is being controlled by Punch ) was almost boring, since I had to skim over all the description. 
 On the bright side, Aaronovitch writes beautifully and is very open-minded. Despite a male main character, there is hardly any sexism, racism or LGBT+ -phobia (if any). That was refreshing and quite nice. 
 If you don't mind a slow building murder mystery and you love magic infused in science, you'll probably love that book."

Review 1 (rated 3/5): "I had never read anything by this author before reading this one. Now that I have, I'm not sure Bared to You isn't gonna be the last one from Day that I'll ever touch. 
 There are people out there claiming that this is 50 Shades with better writing, but I don't agree with that. In my opinion, an author's ability to write encompasses not only the skill of using language structures properly, but also the skills to create believable and interesting characters, express relatable emotions through them and, most importantly, the ability of developing a plot that is exciting and actually makes sense. Sadly, I didn't find any of those traits here. 
 Even though I liked the female lead here, she was not relatable enough and didn't have enough depth to make me really care about her. The male lead had no charisma at all; he was just one of those unrealistic characters created to make women swoon. Also, their relationship started out of nowhere; the female lead didn't like the guy at all and then all of a sudden they were having sex all the time. It didn't feel realistic at all. 
 Actually, that's another point that made my nose twitch at this book: there's too much sex - and yes, that's a thing. I mean, it's ok that this is an erotic book and as such sex should be expected. But when the amount of sex reaches a point where the sentences used to describe it become repetitive to the point of bringing you to boredom, you just know that something's wrong. On the other hand, the scenes where the main characters weren't having sex, but rather flirting with each other, were really good. I think the author should've stuck with that: more sexual tension, less actual sex. 
 So yeah, to put things shortly, this book was rather weird to me. I love dark stories, but some parts were too disturbing. I love erotica, but this had too much sex. Also, the characters felt kinda shallow and the plot not always made sense. You could give it a try if you really can't help it, but I wouldn't recommend it. Maybe I'll read the second instalment someday, but this book didn't give me much motivation to do so. 
 That's it for this one. Cya!"

 In this book, when I saw that a sex scene was coming up, I skipped all the pages and sighed to myself saying, 'Yup, another one.' (Surely I'm not the only one who did this?)

--- COMMUNITY REVIEWS FOR BOOK A: "Eleanor and Park" ---
Community Average Rating: 4.11/5

Review 1 (rated 5/5): "Oh my god I wish I could give this like six and a half stars."

Review 2 (rated 4/5): "3.5 stars 
 I didn't think I would come to really enjoy this book and get hooked with the love story of Eleanor & Park. I thought it would be lame, cheesy, and childish (something that only teenagers can enjoy), but it turned out to be one of the most charming books I've read. It's light but serious, and cute but mature at the same time. It was nice to witness how Eleanor and Park's feelings toward each other blossomed from infatuation to a matured relationship (for their age). I also liked how their characters developed, how their stories unfolded, how they were able to hold their own and dealt with their problems - they felt so real and very relatable."

Review 3 (rated 5/5): "Perfect in every way. 
 The only thing I can say is I wish I had written it."

Review 4 (rated 2/5): "Pretty underwhelming. Didn't find myself caring about the characters all too much and I think I've now realized that I don't particularly enjoy Rowell's writing style."

Review 5 (rated 5/5): "I didn't want it to end. An amazing book. Definitely going on my list of favorites."

Review 6 (rated 5/5): "My favorite YA book in a long time. I'm still processing the book...more to write later."

Review 7 (rated 5/5): "This is the kind of novel that comes along once in a great while that touches you in a way you never imagined. The love story of Eleanor and Park stayed with me long after the last page. Rainbow Rowell does a wonderful job of creating characters that you not only root for, but feel you know them. This is simply a great novel, very well written, wonderful plotting, and can't be recommended enough."

Review 8 (rated 4/5): "Ahhh. First loves. They say they'll change you, that you'll always remember them. But sometimes, they will save you. 
 The story of Eleanor and Park weightlessly lays out the awkward, confusing journey of first loves and adolescent awakenings, bringing you as close as you can to reliving those experiences you can only experience once. 
 A lot of young adult and teen books carry a sense of wisdom in the voice, a part of that childhood innocence lost as the author tries to remember what it was like to be a teen. But Rowell doesn't lose that innocence and can even maintain it when dealing with the heavy side of growing up - broken homes, bullying, abuse. 
 Somehow she manages to bring it all together into a sweet, hopeful, heartbreaking story. One that I read in almost one sitting and never wanted to put down."

Review 2 (rated 1/5): "This is the first Patterson novel I've ever read, and it will be my last. I enjoy police procedurals, but not when the writing is so awkward, and the plot so full of holes. 
 The main character is Doctor-detective Alex Cross who is such a hot-shot super detective that he continuously misidentifies the killer, and makes really poor decisions. 
 There are certain chapters which go into excruciating detail (worryingly, the sex assault/murder chapters are included in this), while there are sudden unexplained gaps in time in other places in the book, which make no sense. 
 Avoid."

Review 3 (rated 3/5): "I never saw the movie so didn't really know what I was getting into with this. Finished it in one night it was that much of a page turner. Definitely not for the faint of heart, or one to read alone though. It is 451 pages of complete creepy, diabolical sadism that will make you want to sleep with the lights on. 
 Would've given it more stars but for a few things...there is a relationship that develops that feels wholly unbelievable given what one of them has gone through. It doesn't seem to give justice to the trauma this person would have gone through. Secondly, how the crime is solved. The initial tip-off to the guilty party seemed to be an afterthought and we're given very little background on how this person ever even came up as a suspect. 
 Solid read, but with some holes. Don't read it alone, or late at night."

Review 4 (rated 1/5): "This is genuinely the worst book I have ever finished. 
 To be fair, it is tolerable when there is action, which is often. But every time James Patterson tries to put words coming out of a characters mouth, it makes you want to punch yourself in the face. When he writes descriptive, emotional paragraphs, it makes you want to punch him in the face. 
 I actually dog-eared a couple pages because the writing was so bad, I wanted to be able to quick reference it to people to show them how bad it was. 
 Want another example of how bad a writer he is? One of his other books is called, "Night of the Machete." I am not a God-fearing man, but if you believe in God, maybe throw in an extra prayer for James Patterson's English language murdering soul."

Review 5 (rated 4/5): "Hold onto your hat, this is a roller coaster ride. Does evil get any more horrible? The bad guys are so clever. There were a couple of times when I had to say, "Really Alex? You are not that stupid." But his dumb moves certainly keep the story raging on. 
 This is James Patterson, in the beginning, on his own, making a name for himself with great writing, intense suspense, awesome characters, and the start of a fabulous Alex Cross series."

Review 6 (rated 5/5): "I can't get enough of the Alex Cross novels by James Patterson!! I own them all, but haven't finished the series yet. 
 I read it because I really liked the movie, and a friend told me that the book was so much more graphic - it was!"

Review 7 (rated 3/5): "A story that is good at building suspense and creating a sense of unease. However, the graphic and gratuitous descriptions of violence against women were deeply unpleasant and misogynistic and it makes me question the author's state of mind. Not sure if I would read another of his books."

Review 8 (rated 3/5): "There is no question that the story itself was creepy, if not terrifying. I did however find that the constant pop culture references from the 90s made it less timeless as a crime thriller. It also had quite a bit of cheesy one liners, and an unnecessary, almost uncomfortable budding romance between a detective and a victim. Aside from it's cheesy pitfalls, the detail in the process of investigating and hunting down the serial killers, was well detailed, and fascinating."
